source.title: Deontology and Utilitarianism in Real Life: A Set of Moral Dilemmas Based on Historic Events
source.changes: De-identified and reworded; incidental details generalised; question in yes/no form.

kept: You are a passenger, not a pilot; a few hijackers claim to have a bomb.
Phone calls reveal other hijacked planes struck buildings; you infer, rather than know, a similar plan for your aircraft.
Non-resistance might lead to a crash into a building that kills all passengers and many others.
Resistance probably prompts killings or detonation, but could divert the fatal crash to an uninhabited area and spare people on the ground.
You intervene directly but the exact resistance method is unspecified; you die along with the other passengers in the stated crash alternatives, with no personal survival gain.
The suggested action is to resist the hijackers.
rewrite: You are a passenger on a domestic flight when a few hijackers seize the aircraft and say they have a bomb. Some passengers phone relatives or friends and learn that other aircraft were hijacked and flown into buildings elsewhere. You think your plane’s hijackers also intend to crash into a building. If you do not resist, they might hit another building, killing everyone aboard and many additional people. If you resist, they will probably start killing passengers or set off their bomb. You could, however, cause the aircraft to crash in an uninhabited area. Everyone aboard would still die, but the additional people would be spared. Do you resist the hijackers?
notes: Deliberately retained: hijacking, the claimed bomb, evidence of prior crashes into buildings, passenger resistance and the uninhabited crash alternative; these determine the inferred threat, probable retaliation and deaths aboard versus on the ground. This causal structure remains recognisable. No moral inference depends on the terrorist label; hijacking and threatened killings remain.

generalised.why: the number of attackers is not a count of victims or beneficiaries
multiple prior crashes remain evidence for the inferred threat
the type and layout of the prior target do not change the inference
seizing the aircraft and threatening lethal violence retain the conduct at stake
